newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FEATURE - Philippine town upbeat on HK job security.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Philippine town upbeat on HK job security.

text.p: Many families in this Philippine farming town send housemaids to work in Hong Kong, and its residents express at least short-term confidence about job security when Chinese rule returns on July 1.
They believe that with the passing of Britain's last colonial outpost in Asia, Hong Kong will remain a haven for job-hunters specialising in domestic chores.

This confidence contrasts with anxieties expressed by thousands of Filipina maids in Hong Kong who fear for their future, worrying that Chinese women from the mainland will take their jobs at lower wages.
Hong Kong authorities have sought to reassure the 140,000 Filipinas, the territory's largest foreign community, about life in an autonomous region of China.

Such is the lure Hong Kong holds for the women of Pozorrubio that, given a chance, 32-year-old Rhodora "Ruby" Sacluti says she is willing to leave her husband and four children behind to try her luck as a domestic there.
"No," she said, when asked if she was afraid of working in Hong Kong after the handover to China at midnight on June 30.
"You don't hold your destiny in your hands," she said with a fatalism typical of rural folk in the Philippines. "It's all a matter of luck. One gets an ace, another a spade."
Sacluti's mother thinks she drew an ace. A young mother when she left for Hong Kong 24 years ago, she is now 55 and still working there for a British expatriate.
She has sent Ruby, her lone child, through college, built a house for her, bought a car and has money in the bank.
MAIDS MIGRATION "TO LAST INTO NEXT MILLENNIUM"
Located 150 km (95 miles) north of Manila, Pozorrubio is a community of 60,000 people whose economy depends to a large extent on the 4,000 Pozorrubians working in foreign countries.
About 700 of the Filipina housemaids in Hong Kong are from Pozorrubio, driven abroad by poverty at home.
"Assuming one worker sends US$100 home once a month, that's $400,000 or more than ten million pesos circulating in Pozorrubio alone monthly," municipal administrator Mel Jovellanos said.
This explains, he said, the growing number of small businesses in the town, from fast-food restaurants to ironworks shops, and the proliferation of TV sets in the humblest homes.
Like other officials, Jovellanos believes the future of Filipina maids -- 75 per cent of whom are college graduates or professionals -- is secure, at least for the time being.
"We're processing more papers of those going to Hong Kong," he said. "Some are leaving next week... This will continue even beyond the year 2000."
One did come back, but not because of concerns about China.
Feeling it was time to settle down in her homeland, Violeta Salazar, 50, returned last year after being away 16-1/2 years.
The "Hong Kong fever" has so infected Salazar's clan that 25 relatives, from her own children to cousins and in-laws, have followed her trail to the colony, to work as maids or drivers.
None has any plans to come home, she said.
"There are some (Filipinos) who are worried because nobody knows what will happen," she said. "But they are staying because they have to... It's a nice feeling to hold money in your hands."
GOOD TIMES WON'T LAST FOREVER
Beijing's pledge to maintain the status quo after the handover has helped ease anxieties.
Philippine labour officials also said it would be difficult to replace the Filipinas because of their work efficiency and their relative fluency in English.
But the good times will not last forever.

"With the handover, border laws are likely to ease up which could fuel an exodus of mainlanders to Hong Kong in search of jobs," labour undersecretary Jose Espanol said. "Their common ethnic and cultural background with the Hong Kong locals could also be an attraction for employment."
Espanol ruled out any prospect of Filipinas returning home in droves soon, saying it would take three to five years of training for Chinese workers to dislodge them.
But even if Hong Kong ceases to be a mecca for maids, there will always be a Hong Kong in Pozorrubio.

It will be in the 24-carat gold ring Salazar wears on her finger and on the gold chain around her neck. It will be in the bungalow Sacluti's mother, Dominga, built for her. And, it will be in a tree-shaded grove created in a corner of the town plaza with the help of money sent by maids.
A sign at its gate reads, "Hongkongers Park."
